payload.analysis: Based on the 10-year progressive bilateral visual field constriction with severe central vision loss and no afferent pupillary defect, chronic bilateral glaucoma remains the leading hypothesis, as it characteristically causes symmetric peripheral field loss. However, the requested core diagnostic data—visual field pattern, optic disc cup-to-disc ratio, intraocular pressure, and OCT retinal nerve fiber layer thickness—were not obtained, so definitive confirmation is lacking. Retinal dystrophy remains a plausible alternative but is less specific. All available clinical information has been integrated, yet confirmatory imaging evidence is incomplete.

payload.report: The patient has 10-year progressive bilateral visual loss with severe field constriction and no afferent pupillary defect, most consistent with chronic bilateral primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG). The absence of bitemporal hemianopia refutes a compressive chiasmal lesion. Fundus autofluorescence hyperfluorescent foci raise retinal dystrophy as an important differential and argue against primary optic neuropathy. However, intraocular pressure, cup-to-disc ratio, OCT retinal nerve fiber layer thickness, and visual field pattern were not obtained, and electroretinography/genetic testing are unavailable, so confidence is moderate. POAG remains the leading diagnosis, but confirmatory ophthalmic testing is required to exclude retinal dystrophy and finalize the diagnosis.
